chief_complaint: inability to sleep for several weeks
hpi_details: 52M presents to the outpatient clinic with a chief complaint of severe insomnia. He was laid off from his job 3 months ago and recently separated from his wife, leading him to drink soju most nights to cope. Upon further questioning, he admits to experiencing daily thoughts of dying for the past 2 weeks. He discloses a concrete suicide plan, having bought charcoal and tape to use in his car. He has no prior suicide attempts and identifies his teenage daughter as his sole protective factor.
ideas: believes his life is falling apart and sees no way out of his current situation
concerns: worries that he will eventually act on his thoughts of dying
expectations: hopes for a sleeping pill to at least get some rest, unaware of the severity of his depression
pmh: No prior psychiatric history or suicide attempts.
social_hx: Recently separated from wife. Unemployed (laid off 3 months ago). Drinks soju most nights. Has one teenage daughter.

boundaries_and_exceptions: In cases of imminent self-harm, breaching patient confidentiality to contact emergency services or family to ensure safety is legally and ethically justified.
If the patient refuses voluntary psychiatric evaluation, involuntary hold procedures (according to local mental health laws) must be initiated.
common_misconceptions: Believing that asking directly about suicide will plant the idea in the patient's head.
Assuming that a patient who came in voluntarily for a minor complaint like insomnia is not at immediate risk of suicide.
Over-relying on a protective factor (like a child) to discharge a patient who has a concrete plan and access to lethal means.
Focusing solely on treating the presenting complaint (prescribing sleep aids) without addressing the underlying severe depression and suicidality.
core_concepts: Direct, specific questioning about suicidal ideation, intent, plan, and access to means is essential for all patients presenting with significant psychosocial stressors or depression.
A concrete suicide plan with available means (e.g., charcoal and tape) in the context of recent losses and alcohol use indicates a high acute risk requiring immediate intervention.

Patients at high acute risk of suicide must not be allowed to leave the clinic alone; urgent same-day psychiatric evaluation and potentially involuntary admission are indicated if safety cannot be guaranteed.
Identifying protective factors, such as family members (e.g., a teenage daughter), is important but does not negate the need for immediate safety measures when a concrete plan and means are present.
dangerous_errors: Allowing a patient with a concrete suicide plan and means to leave the clinic alone or unescorted.
Failing to explicitly ask about suicidal ideation, intent, and access to means.
Prescribing sedative-hypnotic medications to a highly suicidal patient without ensuring safety, as these can be used for overdose or exacerbate impulsivity.
Failing to attempt to contact family or emergency services to secure the patient's immediate safety.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: inability to sleep for several weeks
Key HPI features: 52M with recent major life stressors (job loss, marital separation), increased alcohol consumption, and admitted daily thoughts of dying for 2 weeks.
High-risk indicators: Disclosure of a concrete suicide plan (using charcoal in his car) and active preparation (having already purchased the charcoal and tape).
Relevant background/PMH: No prior psychiatric history, but sudden accumulation of severe psychosocial stressors.
management_principles: Do not leave the patient alone; ensure continuous observation while arranging for urgent transfer.
Arrange for an urgent same-day psychiatric evaluation or admission to a secure psychiatric facility.
Involve family members or emergency contacts (with patient consent when possible, or overriding if imminent danger) to help remove access to lethal means (charcoal, tape, car).
Avoid prescribing medications that could be lethal in overdose or lower impulse control (e.g., large quantities of benzodiazepines) in the outpatient setting.

source_refs.title: American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guideline for the Assessment and Treatment of Patients With Suicidal Behaviors

clinical_knowledge.topic: Major Depressive Disorder with High Acute Suicide Risk

reference_soap.assessment: Major depressive disorder, severe, with high acute suicide risk. The combination of a concrete plan, access to lethal means, recent severe psychosocial stressors, and alcohol use places the patient in imminent danger.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: stable. Patient appears despondent, makes poor eye contact, and has a depressed, tearful affect. Psychomotor retardation noted. Speech is slow. Endorses active suicidal ideation with a specific, concrete plan and access to lethal means. Insight is partial; judgment is severely impaired by depression. No psychotic features elicited.
reference_soap.plan: Maintain 1:1 continuous observation in the clinic. Do not allow the patient to leave alone. Arrange for urgent same-day psychiatric evaluation for inpatient admission (voluntary or involuntary if necessary). Contact emergency services/family to secure the vehicle and remove lethal means (charcoal, tape). Defer prescribing sleep medications at this time.
reference_soap.subjective: 52M presenting with insomnia, reporting daily thoughts of dying for the past 2 weeks following job loss and marital separation. Admits to buying charcoal and tape with the intent to end his life in his car. Drinks soju most nights. Has a teenage daughter whom he cites as his only reason to live.

learning_objectives: Conduct a comprehensive suicide risk assessment, including inquiry about ideation, intent, plan, access to means, and protective factors.
Recognize the clinical presentation of severe major depressive disorder masked by a chief complaint of insomnia.
Implement immediate safety protocols for a patient at high acute suicide risk, including preventing the patient from leaving the facility alone.
Navigate the ethical and clinical considerations of breaching confidentiality to ensure patient safety when imminent risk of harm is identified.

teaching.diagnosis: Major Depressive Disorder, severe, with high acute suicide risk
differentials: Alcohol use disorder with substance-induced depressive disorder

must_ask.say: Have you been having any thoughts of hurting yourself or ending your life?

must_ask.objective: Assess for suicide plan and intent
must_ask.say: Do you have a specific plan for how you would end your life?
Have you gathered any materials or taken any steps to carry out this plan?
Is there anything or anyone that keeps you from acting on these thoughts?
Over the past few weeks, have you been feeling sad, hopeless, or lost interest in things you usually enjoy?
How much alcohol or soju have you been drinking recently to help you cope?
Can you tell me more about your recent job loss and the separation from your wife?

teaching.one_liner: A middle-aged man presenting with insomnia and significant psychosocial stressors, found to have severe depression and a concrete suicide plan involving charcoal, requiring immediate safety intervention.
red_flags: Concrete suicide plan with active preparation (bought charcoal and tape)
Recent severe psychosocial losses (job loss, marital separation)
Daily thoughts of dying for multiple weeks

history.answer: I haven't been able to sleep for weeks, doctor, and lately I keep having thoughts that I just want to die.
For the past two weeks, thoughts of dying come into my head every single day, and I still feel that way right now.
I planned to end my life in my car using charcoal, and the thought won't leave my mind.
I already bought charcoal briquettes and heavy tape, and they are in the trunk of my car right outside.
No, I have never tried to kill myself or hurt myself in the past.
I was laid off from my job three months ago, and then my wife separated from me and moved out.
I feel deeply depressed and empty all day, have lost interest in everything, barely eat, cannot concentrate, and feel completely worthless.
I feel like my life is completely falling apart with no way out, and that I am only a burden to the people around me.
history.topic: Hopelessness and feeling like a burden

history.answer: No, I have never had any period in my life where I felt overly energized, high, or stayed awake for days without feeling tired.
history.topic: Screening for mania or elevated mood

history.answer: No, I do not hear any voices or see things that aren't there, and no one is commanding me to do anything.
I have been drinking a bottle or two of soju almost every night to cope and sleep, but when I drink, the dark thoughts become even worse.
I feel very restless and terrified that I might act on these thoughts, but I have no anger or desire to harm anyone else.
No, I have never experienced physical violence or abuse, and nobody is threatening me right now.
No, I don't suffer from any chronic pain conditions or severe medical illnesses.
No, no one in my family or close circle has ever attempted or died by suicide.
No, I have never seen a psychiatrist or mental health professional, and I've never taken psychiatric medication.
My teenage daughter is the only reason I am holding on right now. I live alone since my wife left, but I cannot bear the thought of abandoning my daughter.
I feel like my whole life has collapsed and there is no way forward, and I am terrified that I will actually end up acting on these thoughts.
I was really hoping you could just give me a sleeping pill so I could finally get some rest.
I don't have any chronic medical conditions like high blood pressure, diabetes, or heart disease.
I have never had any surgeries and I have never been admitted to a hospital.
I don't take any regular prescription medications, over-the-counter drugs, or herbal supplements.
No, I do not have any known allergies to medications or anything else.
I smoke about half a pack of cigarettes a day, and have for about twenty years.
I was an office manager until I was laid off three months ago, and right now I live alone in an apartment.
My parents both had high blood pressure, but there is no family history of depression or mental illness.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 122/78 mmHg, heart rate 74 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, body temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Patient appears visibly despondent, slouched in his chair, tearful, with poor eye contact and evident psychomotor slowing.

Alert and oriented to person, place, and time; speech is noticeably slow; affect is depressed and tearful; thought content shows active suicidal ideation with concrete plan; insight is partial and judgment is severely impaired.
No scars, cuts, hesitation marks, or signs of acute or remote self-harm on wrists, forearms, or neck.
No resting or postural tremors of the hands; mild psychomotor slowing without abnormal involuntary movements.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal first and second heart sounds and no murmurs, gallops, or rubs.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally with no wheezing, rhonchi, or crackles.
Abdomen is soft, non-distended, and non-tender throughout with no rebound tenderness or guarding.
